statement: A named comparative research program exists for modern individually-attributed script inventions, under the term "neography": Piers Kelly (linguistic anthropologist, Max Planck Institute / University of New England), across "The Invention, Transmission and Evolution of Writing: Insights from the New Scripts of West Africa" (2018, covering Vai/Bamum/Masaba comparatively), "The Art of Not Being Legible: Invented Writing Systems as Technologies of Resistance in Mainland Southeast Asia" (2018, covering Pahawh Hmong and other Southeast Asian cases), and "Unsettled Scripts: Script Invention and the Bind of Digital Recognition" (Modern Languages Open). No single Kelly paper treats Cherokee, Vai, Pahawh Hmong, and N'Ko together as one set — each covers a regional subset — so this should be characterized as an active but recent/fragmented research program, not a single canonical synthesis text. Stephen Houston's edited The First Writing: Script Invention as History and Process (Cambridge UP, 2004) covers a different topic (ancient first-writing systems: cuneiform, proto-Elamite, Egyptian, Chinese, Mesoamerican) and should not be cited as covering these modern cases despite the similar title.
